12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
20	
21	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
22	
23	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
24	
25	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
26	
27	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
28	
29	The two suites work in the same way:
30	
31	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
32	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
33	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
34	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
35	
36	To run a suite:
37	
38	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
39	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
40	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
41	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

44	
45	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.

47	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
48	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.

58	  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.

66	
67	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.

69	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
70	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.

1	# The interpreter (walk)
2	
3	Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:
4	
5	- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
6	- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
7	- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
8	- `glue/`: the natives.
9	
10	## How walk evaluates a program
11	
12	After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.
13	
14	At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.
15	
16	Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.
17	
18	Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.
19	
20	- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so a coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` gets `n` = 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
21	- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
22	- A numeral at `=` takes its default. So `u = 0` is `false` for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, and so is `q = 0.5` for `q: QQ = 1/2` (ledger row 973). `u =/= 0` and `q =/= 0.5` are then `true` (ledger row 966). Bind the numeral at the type first, as `z: NN32 = 0`, then write `u = z` or `u =/= z`.
23	- A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, its default, gives `Infinity`, with no error, on both paths (ledger row 980). The rules do not say whether it is an error, so assert no value for it in a test.
24	- A numeral type written in a `comprises` clause loads and runs, as `trait T comprises { NaturalNumeral[\1, 10, 3\] } end` does (ledger row 981). The rules refuse it, as the compiled checker does, and as walk does at load in an `extends` clause or as a static argument: 'NaturalNumeral cannot be written in a program except as a parameter's type.'
25	- A body with a declared return type is not converted by coercion, except a numeral: `r(): Wide = NarrowOf(3)` returns the `NarrowOf` (ledger row 387). Write the value at the declared type.
26	
27	## Where a fix of walk belongs
28	
29	Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
30	
31	- coercion;
32	- chained comparisons;
33	- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
34	- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
35	- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.
36	
37	Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.
38	
39	An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.
40	
41	## What walk checks
42	
43	Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
44	
45	Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.
46	
47	At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:
48	
49	- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for a position where the two parameter types neither nest nor exclude. If a parameter type there mentions a static parameter, the message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". If neither does, it is "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The pairs:
50	  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
51	  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
52	  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations, nor a generic one beside a plain one, nor a generic function beside a generic trait's or object's functional method that has no static parameters of its own;
53	  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.
54	
55	  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
56	  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
57	  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
58	  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
59	  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
60	  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
61	  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
62	  - It does not refuse a type that extends a self-typed trait `T[\A\]` and is not an `A` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). A call that both `T`'s operator and another declaration fit then runs one of them, without an ambiguity error (ledger row 893). Make each type that extends `T[\A\]` an `A`.
63	  - It loads a generic top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's functional method of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. The checker refuses every top-level function more specific than a functional method of its name, a check that the specification does not state: '… is more specific than the declaration of the functional method' (ledger row 894).
64	  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
65	  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).
66	
67	  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. Walk refuses the pair: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker reads the bounds, finds that no value lies in both domains, and accepts it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 713).
68	- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in a type that provides both, where their name is an identifier or an operator named by a word, as `MAX`.
69	- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
70	- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). In another declaration's bound, it takes a name equal to the variable's as the variable (ledger row 778).
71	- a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, where a member's declared type names the variable: "Missing type E" (ledger row 755).
72	- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
73	- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
74	  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
75	  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.
76	
77	  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.
78	
79	So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:
80	
81	- adds an overload;
82	- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
83	- adds an `override` that overrides nothing;

87	Walk checks a program's declarations against the library's only when it analyses the library, not when it loads the library's entries from the cache (ledger row 342). So a program that walk refuses with an empty cache runs with a filled one. Deleting the program's own entries does not bring the check back. To see such a refusal, run with an empty cache, as `COLD_CACHE=1` gives `harness-one.sh`.

89	Walk compares no component with the apis that it exports. So a component that leaves out an api member, or declares it at another header, loads and runs under walk. The compiled export check refuses it (ledger row 841). `library.md`, "Designing a change", gives the step that runs the check on each component.

91	`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.
92	
93	Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.

95	## Natives
96	
97	The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:
98	
99	- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes walk's `FValue` objects, so the compiled path cannot use it.
100	- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives"). Most bindings name a helper. The others name a glue class. F-299 counts both kinds (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
101	
102	Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:
103	
104	- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` and `Float`, the library's object that extends `RR64`, in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;

106	
107	In a method, walk carries `self` by the type that declares the method:
108	
109	- a type of the list above, except `JavaString` and `()`, in the same Java type, but `FlatString` only where it is the library's own;
110	- the library's objects that extend number types, not the glue classes of the same names: `Int` (`ZZ32`) in `int`, `Long` (`ZZ64`) and `UnsignedLong` (`NN64`) in `long`, and `BigNum` (`ZZ`) in `BigInteger`.
111	
112	A program can give its own type the name `FlatString` or `JavaString`. Walk tells the library's `FlatString` by the component that declares it, so a program's own type of either name carries no `self`. But walk carries a parameter declared at such a type in `String`, by the type's name alone, and does not refuse the binding. The native then receives the name of the type, not the value's text (ledger row 877). Give a program's own type another name.
113	
114	Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:
115	
116	- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
117	- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not carried by the first list: 'no Java type carries the declared'.

122

131	
132	    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
133	    return new FortressError(f);

POSITIONS.md:104
- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). The parameter types of the declaration that a call runs are places that fix a type, and a numeral argument goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be, with its default as the last resort: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, the numeral an `NN32` at `NN32`'s own `=` (P-46 gives the rule and its ground; rows 973 and 966 hold where walk departs). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.

== Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:117-199

\subsection{Array Expressions}
\seclabel{array-expr}

Array element expressions are enclosed in brackets. Element expressions
along a row are separated only by whitespace.
Two dimensional array expressions are written by separating rows with
newlines or semicolons.  If a semicolon appears, whitespace before
and after the semicolon is ignored.
The parts of higher-dimensional array expressions are separated
by repeated-semicolons, where the dimensionality
of the result is equal to one plus the number
of repeated semicolons.
The type of a $k$-dimensional array expression is
\EXP{\TYP{Array}k\llbracket{}T, 0, n_{\mathrm{0}}, \cdots,
         0, n_{k-1}\rrbracket},
where \VAR{T} is the union type of the types of the element expressions and
$n_0, ..., n_{k-1}$
are the sizes of the array in each dimension\footnote{
As of March 2008, the Fortress library provides \EXP{\TYP{Array}k} types for
$1 \le k \le 3$.}. This type can be abbreviated as
\EXP{T [n_{\mathrm{0}}, \cdots, n_{k-1}]}.




A $k$-dimensional array \VAR{A} is indexed by placing a sequence of
$k$ indices enclosed in brackets, and separated by commas, after an expression
evaluating to \VAR{A}.
Thus, the index is rendered as a subscript.
By default, arrays are indexed from 0.  The
horizontal dimension of an array is the last dimension mentioned in the
array index.  For example:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.Array.a.tex}
then \EXP{A_{1,0}} evaluates to \EXP{4}.

An array of two
\marginnote{two or more -- Jan: I continue to disbelieve.}
dimensions whose elements are a subtype of \TYP{Number}
is a matrix.
\marginnote{
can be coerced to a matrix.
Matrix types are written
\EXP{\TYP{Matrix}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket [n_{\mathrm{0}} \times \ldots \times n_{k-1}]},
where $k > 1$.
A type of this form can be abbreviated as
\EXP{T^{n_0 \times \ldots \times n_{k-1}}}.}
Matrices are indexed in the same manner as arrays.

A one-dimensional array whose elements are a subtype of \TYP{Number}
is a vector.
\marginnote{
can be coerced to a vector.
Vector types are written \EXP{\TYP{Vector}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket [n]}.
A type of this form can be abbreviated as
\EXP{T^{n}}, unless \VAR{T} is declared in the enclosing scope
to be a physical dimension or unit.

Matrices occurring inside a matrix literal on the same row are
pasted along dimension 0. Each row is pasted along dimension 1 and the
resulting matrix is ``flattened''.  This works because matrices never
contain other matrices as elements.
}

The element expressions in an array expression may be either scalars or
array expressions themselves.  If an element is an array expression,
it is ``flattened'' (pasted) into the enclosing expression.
This pasting works because array expressions never
contain other arrays as elements.  The elements along
a row (or column) must have the same number of columns (or rows),
though two elements in different rows (columns) need not have the
same number of columns (rows).
See \secref{unpasting} for a discussion of matrix unpasting.

\section{Top-Level Variable Declarations}
\seclabel{top-var-decls}
\begin{Grammar}
\emph{VarDecl}
&::=& \option{\emph{VarMods}} \emph{VarWTypes} \emph{InitVal} \\
&$|$& \option{\emph{VarImmutableMods}} \emph{BindIdOrBindIdTuple} \EXP{=} \emph{Expr}\\
&$|$& \option{\emph{VarMods}} \emph{BindIdOrBindIdTuple} \EXP{\mathrel{\mathtt{:}}} \emph{Type}\EXP{...}
\emph{InitVal} \\
&$|$& \option{\emph{VarMods}} \emph{BindIdOrBindIdTuple} \EXP{\mathrel{\mathtt{:}}} \emph{TupleType}
\emph{InitVal} \\

\emph{VarMods} &::=& \emph{VarMod}$^+$\\

\emph{VarImmutableMods} &::=& \emph{VarImmutableMod}$^+$\\

\emph{VarMod} &::=& \emph{AbsVarMod} $|$ \KWD{private}\\

\emph{VarImmutableMod} &::=& \emph{AbsVarImmutableMod} $|$ \KWD{private}\\

\emph{AbsVarMod} &::=& \KWD{var} $|$ \KWD{test}\\

\emph{AbsVarImmutableMod} &::=& \KWD{test}\\

\emph{VarWTypes} &::=& \emph{VarWType} \\
&$|$& \texttt{(} \emph{VarWType}(\EXP{,} \emph{VarWType})$^+$ \texttt{)}\\

\emph{VarWType} &::=& \emph{BindId} \emph{IsType}\\

\emph{InitVal} &::=& (\EXP{=}$|$\EXP{\ASSIGN}) \emph{Expr} \\

\emph{TupleType} &::=&
\texttt{(} \emph{Type}\EXP{,} \emph{TypeList} \texttt{)}\\

\emph{TypeList} &::=& \emph{Type}(\EXP{,} \emph{Type})$^*$ \\

\emph{IsType} &::=& \EXP{\mathrel{\mathtt{:}}} \emph{Type}\\
\end{Grammar}

A \emph{variable}'s name can be any valid Fortress identifier.
There are three forms of variable declarations.  The first form:
%id : Type = expr
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{id} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Type} = \VAR{expr}\)
\end{Fortress}
declares \VAR{id} to be an immutable variable with static type \TYP{Type}
whose value is computed to be the value of the \emph{initializer} expression
\VAR{expr}.
The static type of \VAR{expr} must be a subtype of \TYP{Type}.


The second (and most convenient) form:
%id = expr
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{id} = \VAR{expr}\)
\end{Fortress}
declares \VAR{id} to be an immutable variable
whose value is computed to be the value of the expression \VAR{expr};
the static type of the variable is the static type of \VAR{expr}.

The third form:
%var id : Type = expr
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{var} \VAR{id} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Type} = \VAR{expr}\)
\end{Fortress}
declares \VAR{id} to be a mutable variable of type \TYP{Type}
whose initial value is computed to be the value of the expression \VAR{expr}.
As before, the static type of \VAR{expr} must be a subtype of \TYP{Type}.
The modifier \KWD{var} is optional
when `\EXP{\ASSIGN}' is used instead of `\EXP{=}' as follows:

%var? id : Type := expr
\begin{Fortress}
\(\option{\KWD{var}}\ \VAR{id} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Type} \ASSIGN \VAR{expr}\)
\end{Fortress}

In short, immutable variables are declared and initialized by `\EXP{=}'
and mutable variables are declared and initialized either by `\EXP{\ASSIGN}'
or by declaring them according to the third form above with the modifier
\KWD{var}.


All forms can be used with \emph{tuple notation} to declare multiple
variables together.  Variables to declare
are enclosed in parentheses and separated by commas, as are the
types declared for them:
%(id(, id)^+) : (Type(, Type)^+)
\begin{Fortress}
\((\VAR{id}(, \VAR{id})^+) \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} (\TYP{Type}(, \TYP{Type})^+)\)
\end{Fortress}
Alternatively, the types can be included alongside the respective variables,
optionally eliding types that can be inferred from context:
%(id(: Type)?(, id(: Type)?)^+)
\begin{Fortress}
\((\VAR{id}\options{\COLON \TYP{Type}}(, \VAR{id}\options{\COLON \TYP{Type}})^+)\)
\end{Fortress}

Alternatively, a single type followed by `\EXP{\ldots}'
can be declared for all of the variables:
%(id(, id)^+): Type...
\begin{Fortress}
\((\VAR{id}(, \VAR{id})^+)\COLON \TYP{Type}\ldots\)
\end{Fortress}
This notation is especially helpful when a function application returns a tuple of values.

The initializer expressions of top-level variable declarations can refer to
variables declared later in textual order.
\label{decl-io}
Evaluation of top-level initializer expressions cannot call
functionals with the modifier \KWD{io}.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored

(*******************************************************************************
    A top-level variable declared with an array type and bound to an array
    literal is the array that the same declaration gives in a function body.
    aggregate.tex, subsection "Array Expressions"; variables.tex, section
    "Top-Level Variable Declarations".
 ******************************************************************************)
component TopLevelArrayLiteral
export Executable

(* A top-level initializer may read a variable declared later. *)
early: ZZ32 = shp[0] + shp[2]

shp: ZZ32[3] = [27 16 27]

grid: ZZ32[3,2] = [1 2; 3 4; 5 6]

(vocabSize, nEmbd) = (27, 16)

dims: ZZ32[2,2] = [vocabSize nEmbd; (4 nEmbd) nEmbd]

names: String[9] = ["wte" "wpe" "attn_wq" "attn_wk" "attn_wv" "attn_wo" "mlp_fc1" "mlp_fc2" "lm_head"]

vec: Vector[\ZZ32,3\] = [1 2 3]

halves: RR64[3] = [1 2 0.5]

counts: NN32[2] = [1 2]

var tally: ZZ32[2] = [5 6]

second(): ZZ32 = shp[1]

run(): () = do
    assert(shp[1], 16, "shp[1]")
    assert(shp[0] + shp[2], 54, "shp[0] + shp[2]")
    assert(|shp|, 3, "|shp|")
    assert(second(), 16, "read in a function")
    assert(early, 54, "read by an earlier initializer")

    assert(grid[2,0], 5, "grid[2,0]")
    assert(grid[0,1], 2, "grid[0,1]")
    assert(grid[1,1], 4, "grid[1,1]")

    assert(dims[0,0], 27, "dims[0,0]")
    assert(dims[0,1], 16, "dims[0,1]")
    assert(dims[1,0], 64, "dims[1,0]")
    assert(dims[1,1], 16, "dims[1,1]")

    assert(names[0], "wte", "names[0]")
    assert(names[8], "lm_head", "names[8]")
    assert(|names|, 9, "|names|")

    assert(vec[2], 3, "vec[2]")
    assert(vec DOT vec, 14, "vec DOT vec")

    h: RR64 = 0.5
    one: RR64 = 1
    assert(halves[2], h, "halves[2]")
    assert(halves[0], one, "halves[0], a numeral at RR64")

    two: NN32 = 2
    assert(counts[1], two, "counts[1], a numeral at NN32")

    assert(tally[1], 6, "tally[1]")
    tally[0] := 9
    assert(tally[0], 9, "tally[0] after an assignment")

    (* The same declarations in a function body. *)
    lshp: ZZ32[3] = [27 16 27]
    lgrid: ZZ32[3,2] = [1 2; 3 4; 5 6]
    assert(lshp[1], shp[1], "the body's literal, rank 1")
    assert(lgrid[2,0], grid[2,0], "the body's literal, rank 2")
end

end
EOF

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
42	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
43	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
44	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
45	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
46	
47	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
48	
49	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
50	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.

1	# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code
2	
3	**seeding**
4	: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
5	
6	**base build**
7	: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.
8	
9	**old code**
10	: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.
11	
12	Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.
13	
14	## Finding or building a base build
15	
16	- If your brief names a base build, use it.
17	- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
18	  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
19	  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
20	  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
21	- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.
22	
23	      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
24	      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
25	      ant compileAll
26	      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
27	      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
28	      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean
29	
30	If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.
31	
32	## Seeding a worktree
33	
34	A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.
35	
36	Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.
37	
38	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
39	
40	- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
41	- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
42	- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
43	- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
44	- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
45	- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
46	- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
47	- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.
48	
49	## Running the old code
50	
51	If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.
52	
53	`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
54	
55	    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
56	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
57	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
58	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
59	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM
60	
61	- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
62	- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
63	- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
64	- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).
65

67	
68	    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
69	        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss
70	
71	The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
117	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
118	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
119	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

block's declaration uses, which LHSEvaluator now shares as libraryArray.

initialization carries the declared type. An element that the array
refuses is reported with its message, and a literal whose size is not
the declared type's is refused at the binding.

## The ladder regression

The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:

- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.

A file that moved gets a mark:

- DOWN: a phase lower than the record.
- MISSING: a file with no output.
- STDOUT: output that differs from the record after the `Operation took <n>ms` line is masked.
- UP: a phase higher than the record. This is progress, not red.

DOWN, MISSING and STDOUT are red, unless your brief declared that move as expected before the gate ran.
Warning: do not run `run-ladder.sh`, the driver over every test program, with its defaults. Its default root is shared, its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run, and its default `OUT` is a tracked folder.

To run it, as step 7, with step 3's copies of the caches:

1. Copy the drivers into `tmp/gate/ladder/`, and point their outputs and caches there:

       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; B=explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19
       cp explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh \
          $B/classify.py $B/microgpt-phase.sh $B/microgpt-phase.py $D/
       sed -i -e "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=$D|" -e "s|^LADDER_ROOT=.*|LADDER_ROOT=$D/root|" $D/run-subset.sh
       sed -i -e "s|/home/user/fortress|$PWD|g" \
           -e "s|^export LADDER_CACHES=.*|export LADDER_CACHES=$D/root/ladder-caches|" \
           -e "s|^export LADDER_TMP=.*|export LADDER_TMP=$D/root/ladder-tmp|" \
           -e "s|^RAW=.*|RAW=$D/raw/microgpt|" -e "s|^TSV=.*|TSV=$D/microgpt-results.tsv|" $D/microgpt-phase.sh
       tail -n +2 $B/pass-list.txt | cut -f1 | sed 's|/|\t|' > $D/subset.txt

2. Run the four scripts, with no arguments, in this order: `bash $D/run-subset.sh`, `python3 $D/classify.py`, `bash $D/microgpt-phase.sh` and `python3 $D/microgpt-phase.py`. Each reads and writes in `$D`. This takes about 200 s for the 85 and 35 s for the eighteen, so run them in the background (`session.md`, "Long commands"). With step 3's copies, the driver skips the library's build (about 145 s).
3. Compare: `ladder_compare $B $D`, then `diff <(mg_phases $B/microgpt-phase.md) <(mg_phases $D/microgpt-phase.md)`. Append each line that they print to the summary, with `# ladder ` before it.

If your brief asks for your change's own ladder subset, write your own `subset.txt`. Put in it each file whose recorded first error in the baseline's `raw/` names something that your change touched. Run them after your edit only. Compare them with the newest landed `ladder.tsv`, or with the baseline's `raw/` for a file that the gate does not run.

== explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md:261-293

## 13. Commands worked out

**The demo driver.** It runs from the tree's root, after the setup lines, as `run-demos.sh <out-dir>`:

    set -u
    FH=$PWD ; OUT=$1 ; case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$FH/$OUT" ;; esac ; mkdir -p "$OUT"
    cd "$FH/ProjectFortress/demos"
    LIST=$(ls *.fss | grep -v -E 'Syntax\.fss$|DynamicSemantics\.fss$|Satisfiability\.fss$|GenomeUtil')
    : > "$OUT/summary.tsv"
    for f in $LIST ; do
      n=${f%.fss}
      case "$n" in
        wordcount2) ( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 15 600 bin/fortress ProjectFortress/demos/$f < /dev/null ) > "$OUT/$n.txt" 2>&1 ; rc=$? ;;
        tennisRanking) timeout -k 15 600 ../../bin/fortress $f "$FH/ProjectFortress/demos/tennis050307" "$FH/ProjectFortress/demos/tennis051707" "$FH/ProjectFortress/demos/tennisGames" < /dev/null > "$OUT/$n.txt" 2>&1 ; rc=$? ;;
        *) timeout -k 15 600 ../../bin/fortress $f < /dev/null > "$OUT/$n.txt" 2>&1 ; rc=$? ;;
      esac
      if grep -qi fail "$OUT/$n.txt" ; then fl=fail-in-output ; else fl=clean ; fi
      if [ $rc -eq 0 ] && [ $fl = clean ] ; then v=END ; elif [ $rc -eq 124 ] || [ $rc -eq 137 ] ; then v=LIMIT ; else v=STOP ; fi
      printf '%s\t%s\trc=%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$n" "$v" "$rc" "$fl" "$(grep -v '^ *$' "$OUT/$n.txt" | tail -1 | cut -c1-160)" >> "$OUT/summary.tsv"
    done
    echo "demos: $(grep -c . "$OUT/summary.tsv") run, $(awk -F'\t' '$2=="END"' "$OUT/summary.tsv" | wc -l) reached their end"

**The checker's driver over one demo.** It runs from the tree's root, as steps 1 and 2 of `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh` with the one target:

1. Make `$S/shadow-src` with `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/shadow-patch.py ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress $S/shadow-src && python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/add-patch.py $S/shadow-src`.
2. Compile the seven shadow sources and `DistanceMulti.java`, as `run.sh:102-112` does.
3. Run the driver:

       java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow -Djava.io.tmpdir=$S/tmp -Dfortress.caches=$S/caches \
            -Dprobe.tolerant=true -Dprobe.all=true -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false \
            -cp $S/shadow-classes:$S/classes:$CP DistanceMulti -order check -setting any ProjectFortress/demos/trips.fss

`CP` is the class path that `run.sh` makes from `bin/fortress_classpath`. The driver's own line reported 53 s for the target before the repair, under `nice -n 19`, nproc 4.

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

A literal whose size is not the declared type's is refused at load, 'Type mismatch binding __DefaultVector[\ZZ32,3\] ... to shp (type Array1[\ZZ32,0,4\])', and an element that the array refuses is reported, 'Unification error: ... got arg "a" of type String'.

    Tests run: 3,  Failures: 3,  Errors: 0

    An untyped top-level literal is still bound as its paste, a tuple of tuples at rank 2, with no error at the binding; its first use fails ('RHS does not yield a tuple', 'Non-object receiver'): row 49.

Rows 49 and 104: no note; no test of theirs changed (`ProjectFortress/tests/XXXArrayLiteralArgRungC.fss` still reports its expected failure in the suite's run).

New rows, for section "9. Arrays, vectors and matrices" (NEW-B-1) and "3. Traits, objects and components" (NEW-B-2, beside row 323); each line passes `ledger.py check --rows` but for its number:

| NEW-B-1 | under walk an array literal bound in a block to a declared array type of another size is not refused: `a: ZZ32[4] = [27 16 27]` binds an array of three elements, and `a[1]` is 16; the same declaration at the top level is refused | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (walk) | `Specification/basic/variables.tex`, "Top-Level Variable Declarations"; `Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex`, "Array Expressions" | none | climb batch 32 rung B | siblings: 49, 104. `LHSEvaluator.forLValue` stores the array that `libraryArray` builds at the literal's own extents and never compares it with the declared type (`LHSEvaluator.java:204-206` at 06b90ba6cf); the top-level binding checks it in `BuildEnvironments.forVarDecl4`, 'Type mismatch binding __DefaultVector[\ZZ32,3\] ... to shp (type Array1[\ZZ32,0,4\])' (test `TopLevelArrayLiteralSize`). Rung B: under walk a top-level array literal with a declared type is an array (row 142 closed, 06b90ba6cf, `tests/TopLevelArrayLiteral.fss`); untyped top-level literals stay pastes (row 49); two new rows, a block's literal of the wrong size (NEW-B-1) and a forward read of a later `var` (NEW-B-2, `tests/XXXTopLevelVarForwardRead.fss`).

## Revival change

**The change.** The team's walk bound a top-level variable declared with an array type to the literal's paste, a tuple, and stopped: `shp: ZZ32[3] = [27 16 27]` gave 'Type mismatch binding (27,16,27): (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32) (type (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)) to shp (type Array1[\ZZ32,0,3\])'; only a declaration in a block built the array (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/LHSEvaluator.java:170-207`, the block's binding; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java:788-803`, the top-level check, which built nothing). The tree now builds a top-level literal with a declared array type into the library array of that type, for an immutable and a `var` variable, with numerals, names, expressions, strings or pasted arrays as elements; a reader above the declaration sees the array; a literal of another size than its declared type, or with an element that is not of the element type, is refused at load. Test: `ProjectFortress/tests/TopLevelArrayLiteral.fss`, with `TopLevelArrayLiteralSize` and `TopLevelArrayLiteralElement` for the refusals. The reason: the specification gives an array expression one type wherever it stands, `Arrayk[\T, 0, n0, ...\]` (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex`, "Array Expressions"), and a top-level declaration `id : Type = expr` the same meaning as a local one (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`, "Top-Level Variable Declarations"). Still so: a top-level literal without a declared type is bound as its paste and fails at its first use; write the type. A literal in a block of another size than its declared type is not refused.

**Provenance.** Ledger row 142; the batch's fork B1, "A typed array literal at the top level is the array that the same literal is in a function body", built within P-87 (no model line changes) and P-173 (a numeral element converts at the element type); climb batch 32, rung B.
EOF

## What the specification settles

`aggregate.tex`, "Array Expressions": an array expression has the type `Arrayk[\T, 0, n0, ...\]` wherever it stands. `variables.tex`, "Top-Level Variable Declarations": `id : Type = expr` declares a variable whose value is the value of `expr`, whose static type must be a subtype of `Type`; "The initializer expressions of top-level variable declarations can refer to variables declared later in textual order." So the typed literal is an array, a literal of another size is an error, and a read from above sees the array. The specification does not say how a rank-3 literal's `;;` dimension is indexed beyond "the horizontal dimension of an array is the last dimension mentioned in the array index".

# Rung B, rung-toplevel-array-literal: an array literal with a declared type at the top level is an array under walk

- problem: under walk `shp: Vector[\ZZ32,9\] = [27 16 27 ...]` at the top level fails with 'Type mismatch binding (27,16,...)', while the same declaration in a function body works (ledger row 142): explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:769
- spec: "The type of a k-dimensional array expression is Arrayk[\T, 0, n0, ..., 0, nk-1\]", and `id : Type = expr` at the top level: Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:130 and Specification/basic/variables.tex:58
- precedent: the typed cell of a top-level variable, which converts the value to the declared type when it is first forced (commit b628871a26): ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/env/LazilyEvaluatedCell.java:37
- deviation: the block's code refuses neither a wrong size nor, with a message of its own, a wrong element; the top level refuses both, the size by the check `forVarDecl4` already had, the element by a wrap in `topLevelArray`: ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/LHSEvaluator.java:160
- historical: ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java, ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/LHSEvaluator.java, ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/env/LazilyEvaluatedCell.java: ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/env/LazilyEvaluatedCell.java:71

## What changed and why

Commit 06b90ba6cf, on `wip/rung-toplevel-array-literal`, cut from db352c1776. Three files of walk, four tests.

Walk evaluates an array literal to a paste, an `IUOTuple` (`Evaluator.forArrayElements`). In a block, `LHSEvaluator.forLValue` builds a paste into a library array when the variable has a declared type that is the array trait of the paste's rank. At the top level nothing built it: an immutable variable's cell (`LazilyEvaluatedCell`) kept the paste, and `BuildEnvironments.forVarDecl4` then compared the paste with the declared type and stopped.

1. `LHSEvaluator.libraryArray(paste, declared, at)` (`LHSEvaluator.java:120-152`) is the block's building code, moved out of `forLValue` unchanged: the element type from the declared type, the factory `arrayK[\T, sizes\]()` at the paste's extents, the copy. It returns null where the declared type is not the array trait of the paste's rank. `forLValue` calls it (`:204-206`) and keeps its other arms as they were.
2. `LHSEvaluator.topLevelArray` (`:154-168`) calls it for a top-level variable: it returns the paste itself where nothing is built, so that `forVarDecl4`'s 'Type mismatch binding' stays the report, and it reports an element that the array refuses as 'Unification error: ...' at the literal, as `Evaluator.invokeMethod` and `Fcn.functionInvocation` do for a call (`Evaluator.java:1047-1053`). Without the wrap the run printed `null`: no call encloses a top-level binding, and the `UnificationError` lost its message on its way out of the task pool.
3. `LazilyEvaluatedCell.getValueNull` (`LazilyEvaluatedCell.java:71-74`) builds the literal of an immutable variable declared with a type when the cell is first forced, before the coercion to the declared type that the cell already made. So every reader sees the array: an initializer above the declaration, a function, an importer, and `forVarDecl4`'s check, which now passes, or refuses an array of another size.
4. `BuildEnvironments.forVarDecl4`, mutable arm (`BuildEnvironments.java:764-767`), builds a `var` variable's literal before its type check. `forVarDecl3` (`:718-723`) gives the cell that a `var` holds before its initialization the declared type, so that an initializer above it that subscripts the variable sees the array and not the paste.

No library file, no model line, nothing of the compiled path.

## The failing run and the passing run

The tests were written first and run through the harness in the worktree while it held the base's build and no edit (2026-11-16T02:38:00Z, tree db352c1776), then, after each addition to the tests, on the base build's code:

    FORTRESS_HOME=/home/user/fortress-base33 /home/user/fortress-base33/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh $PWD/tmp/old-harness ProjectFortress/tests/TopLevelArrayLiteral.fss ProjectFortress/tests/TopLevelArrayLiteralSize.fss ProjectFortress/tests/TopLevelArrayLiteralSize.test ProjectFortress/tests/TopLevelArrayLiteralElement.fss ProjectFortress/tests/TopLevelArrayLiteralElement.test

(The base build's worktree is at 84f1c37190, a commit of `explorations/` only before db352c1776; its code is the base's.) The last run after the last change of code:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh $PWD/tmp/h1 <the same five files> ProjectFortress/tests/XXXTopLevelVarForwardRead.fss
